issues.legal_issue: A contractual licence is revocable where its express terms provide for a limited term and do not create an interest in the property.
material_facts: The written agreement granted a licence for a fixed initial term, later extended twice, and required delivery of the premises upon expiry or termination.
The agreement stated that it created no other right or interest in the premises and incorporated the public-premises eviction regime.
The licensee claimed that its investment in constructing a restaurant made the licence irrevocable.
issues.conclusion: The licence was revocable under its terms, and the licensee’s investment did not make it irrevocable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 52 of the Indian Easement Act, 1882, a licence is a right to do something on another’s immovable property that would otherwise be unlawful, without creating an easement or an interest in the property. Whether a contractual licence is revocable ordinarily depends on its express terms, subject to the circumstances expressly provided for in the Act. The Court relied on Muskett v. Hill (1839) 5 Bing (NC) 694 and Heap v. Hartley (1889) 42 Ch. Div. 461.

predicates.contractual_licence_proceeding: The case concerns a claim about whether a contractual licence to use immovable property is revocable.
predicates.fixed_term_in_written_agreement: The grantor and licensee recorded a limited term for the licence in a written agreement.
predicates.agreement_denies_property_interest: The written agreement states that the licence creates no interest or other right in the property.

issues.definition: When a case concerns a contractual licence and the written agreement sets a limited term while denying any property interest, the licence is revocable.

issues.legal_issue: An alleged oral assurance cannot extend a statutory body’s licence when the governing framework requires contracts to be made through prescribed formalities.
material_facts: The airport authority was a statutory corporation empowered to contract subject to statutory requirements and regulations governing the execution of contracts.
The licensee alleged an oral assurance that the licence would be extended and made irrevocable, but no such extension was executed in the prescribed written form.
The restaurant was operational before the initial licence term expired, so the construction investment did not depend on the alleged later assurance.
issues.conclusion: The alleged oral assurance had no legal effect and could not bind the airport authority or extend the licence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 20 and 21 of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 govern the authority’s power to contract and the manner of executing contracts. The Airports Authority of India (Contract) Regulations, 2003, made under the Act, require contracts to be finalized through formal instruments executed by the authority and the other party. A statutory corporation is bound by its governing Act and regulations, so an alleged oral assurance inconsistent with those formalities cannot bind it.

predicates.licence_extension_proceeding: The case concerns a claim that a licence was extended beyond its written term.
predicates.statutory_body_is_bound_by_contract_form: The grantor is a statutory body whose contracts must comply with prescribed execution formalities.
predicates.alleged_extension_is_only_oral: The claimed extension rests on an oral assurance rather than a contract executed in the prescribed form.

issues.definition: In a licence-extension case, an oral assurance does not extend the licence when the grantor is bound by contract formalities and the alleged extension was not formally executed.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant who abandons a position to obtain a procedural benefit cannot later take the inconsistent position after receiving that benefit.
material_facts: The licensee initially sought a declaration that its licence was irrevocable.
After the suit was returned on a jurisdictional ground, the licensee represented that it would delete that declaration and the supporting pleadings.
The suit was revived and proceeded after that representation, and the licensee later again asserted that the licence was irrevocable.
issues.conclusion: The licensee could not revive its abandoned claim that the licence was irrevocable after obtaining the benefit of proceeding on the contrary position.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of election and the rule against approbating and reprobating are facets of estoppel. A litigant who unequivocally chooses a position, communicates it, and obtains a benefit on that basis may be held to that choice. The Court relied on Benjamin Scarf v. Alfred George Jardine (1881–82) 7 Appeal Cases 345; Tinkler v. Hilder (1849) 4 Exch 187; Clough v. London and North Western Rail Co. [(1861–73) All ER, Reprint, 646]; Harrison v. Wells [1966 (3) All ER 524]; Kok Hoong v. Leong Cheong Kweng Mines Ltd. [1964 Appeal Cases 993]; Dwijendra Narain Roy v. Joges Chandra De [AIR 1924 Cal 600]; C. Beepathumma v. V.S. Kadambolithaya [1964 (5) SCR 836]; and M/s New Bihar Biri Leaves Co. v. State of Bihar [(1981) 1 SCC 537].

rule.if: civil_litigation_proceeding and litigant_communicated_clear_election and court_granted_benefit_on_that_basis and later_inconsistent_position

predicates.civil_litigation_proceeding: The dispute involves a litigant taking positions in court proceedings.
predicates.litigant_communicated_clear_election: The litigant clearly communicated a choice between inconsistent positions to the court or the opposing side.
predicates.court_granted_benefit_on_that_basis: The court allowed the proceeding or granted relief after relying on the litigant’s communicated choice.
predicates.later_inconsistent_position: The litigant later advanced a position inconsistent with the one on which the benefit was obtained.

issues.definition: A litigant is bound by a communicated choice when the court grants a benefit on that basis and the litigant later advances an inconsistent position.

issues.legal_issue: An estate officer does not breach natural justice by refusing to summon witnesses to prove an oral assurance that contradicts the governing written documents.
material_facts: In an eviction inquiry, the licensee sought to summon airport-authority officers to support its claim of an oral licence extension.
The written agreement and other documents showed the licence term and contained no written extension beyond the final extended term.
The estate officer gave reasons for declining to summon the officers, and the Court found that the alleged oral assurance could not alter the written terms under the applicable statutory framework.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to summon the officers did not violate natural justice and did not warrant interference.
issues.legal_principle: A hearing authority need not receive evidence that cannot affect the decision because it contradicts governing written documents and cannot establish a legally effective extension. The Court applied the statutory contracting framework under Sections 20 and 21 of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 and the Airports Authority of India (Contract) Regulations, 2003, together with the requirements of a fair hearing.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_inquiry: The proceeding asks an estate officer to determine whether a person occupies public premises without authority.
predicates.written_terms_control_licence_period: The governing written agreement records the licence term and no effective written extension contradicts it.
predicates.requested_witnesses_would_support_contra: The party asks to summon witnesses to prove an oral assurance inconsistent with the written terms.

issues.definition: In a public-premises eviction inquiry, refusing to summon witnesses to prove a contrary oral assurance is not unfair when the written terms control the licence period.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of unequal treatment cannot establish discrimination when the claimant has no legal entitlement to the treatment sought.
material_facts: The licensee alleged that other licensees received extensions while its own licence was not further extended.
Its licence had already been extended twice, and the Court found its assertion about the treatment of other licensees factually incorrect.
The licensee had no legal right to a further extension.
issues.conclusion: The licensee could not establish discrimination or negative equality because it had no legal right to a further extension.
issues.legal_principle: A discrimination claim can assist a person only in enforcing a legal right to particular treatment; unequal treatment does not create an entitlement to treatment that the claimant has no right to demand. The Court rejected the asserted claim of negative equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.equal_treatment_claim: A person alleges that others received treatment that was denied to that person.
predicates.claimant_lacks_legal_entitlement_to_requ: The person has no legal right to the treatment sought.

issues.definition: An equal-treatment claim fails when the claimant has no legal entitlement to the treatment that others allegedly received.

issues.legal_issue: An estate officer’s inquiry into unauthorized occupation need not be widened to decide an unrelated discrimination claim or permit inspection sought for that purpose.
material_facts: The estate officer was deciding whether the licensee was in unauthorized occupation of public premises.
The licensee sought inspection of documents in connection with its discrimination claim.
The estate officer confined the inquiry to unauthorized occupation, and the Court found that limitation proper.
issues.conclusion: The estate officer properly declined to widen the inquiry to include the discrimination claim and the related document-inspection request.
issues.legal_principle: The estate officer’s inquiry under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 is directed to determining unauthorized occupation; it need not be expanded to adjudicate a claim outside that inquiry. The Court also held that the asserted discrimination did not assist the licensee because it had no legal right to a further extension.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_inquiry: The proceeding asks an estate officer to determine whether a person occupies public premises without authority.
predicates.requested_issue_is_outside_unauthorized_: The party asks the officer to decide an issue that is not necessary to determine whether occupation is unauthorized.
predicates.document_request_relates_to_that_issue: The requested document inspection is directed to the outside issue rather than the unauthorized-occupation determination.

issues.definition: An estate officer may limit the inquiry and decline related document inspection when the requested issue is outside the determination of unauthorized occupation.

issues.legal_issue: An estate officer appointed by designation is validly authorized when the governing appointment identifies that designation and the officer holds it.
material_facts: The Central Government had published a notification appointing estate officers by designation for the relevant purpose.
A later published notification substituted the designation of Deputy General Manager (Land Management) for the earlier designation.
The officer who decided the matter held the substituted designation.
issues.conclusion: The officer was validly authorized to act as estate officer by virtue of holding the designation specified in the notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 empowers the Central Government to appoint estate officers. The appointment may be made by designation rather than by naming an individual; an officer holding the designation specified in the operative notification may exercise the office’s functions.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The matter concerns an officer exercising authority in a proceeding about occupation of public premises.
predicates.appointment_notification_names_office_by: The appointing authority’s published notification identifies the relevant office by designation rather than by an individual’s name.
predicates.decision_maker_holds_that_designation: The officer who made the decision held the designation identified in the operative notification.

issues.definition: In a public-premises eviction proceeding, an officer is validly authorized when the appointment notification identifies the office by designation and the decision-maker holds that designation.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory appeal against an estate officer’s order remains available when the Supreme Court retains the related proceeding and expressly preserves the right to challenge that order.
material_facts: The Supreme Court directed a newly appointed estate officer to hear the parties and decide the matter within a specified timeframe.
The Court kept the pending proceedings before it and expressly permitted the parties to challenge or support the estate officer’s eventual order in those proceedings.
After the estate officer made an order, the licensee filed an appeal under the statutory appeal provision, and the Court directed that appeal to be transferred to it.
issues.conclusion: The pending proceedings had not become infructuous, and the licensee’s right to file the statutory appeal had not been taken away; the appeal was transferred to the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: A court’s retention of related proceedings and directions for a new administrative decision do not, without more, extinguish a statutory right of appeal. The Court relied on the terms of its directions preserving the parties’ ability to challenge the resulting order and directed transfer of the appeal so the matters could be considered together.

rule.if: pending_appellate_proceeding and court_retains_seisin and court_preserves_challenge_to_later_order and party_files_statutory_appeal_from_later_order

predicates.pending_appellate_proceeding: A court proceeding challenging an earlier decision remains pending.
predicates.court_retains_seisin: The court keeps control of the related matter while a new decision is made.
predicates.court_preserves_challenge_to_later_order: The court expressly permits the parties to challenge the decision that will be made during the pending proceeding.
predicates.party_files_statutory_appeal_from_later_: A party files an appeal provided by law against the new decision.

issues.definition: A statutory appeal remains available when the court retains the related proceeding, expressly preserves challenges to the later decision, and a party appeals that decision.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may impose costs when a litigant takes inconsistent positions and dishonestly prolongs proceedings.
material_facts: The licensee abandoned its claim that the licence was irrevocable to revive its suit, later again asserted that claim, and pursued inconsistent positions in multiple proceedings.
The inconsistent positions allowed the licensee to retain possession after the licence expired and prolonged proceedings for more than a decade.
The Court found that the licensee had not pursued its proceedings honestly.
issues.conclusion: The Court dismissed the licensee’s appeal with costs payable to the Supreme Court Mediation Center.
issues.legal_principle: The rule against approbating and reprobating prevents a litigant from obtaining benefits through inconsistent positions. The Court treated the litigant’s inconsistent conduct and dishonest prolongation of proceedings as warranting an award of costs, relying on the doctrine of election and approbation and reprobation discussed in Benjamin Scarf, Tinkler, Clough, Harrison, Kok Hoong, Dwijendra Narain Roy, C. Beepathumma, and New Bihar Biri Leaves.

predicates.appellate_litigation_proceeding: The court is deciding an appeal arising from litigation in which a party has taken positions before courts or tribunals.
predicates.litigant_takes_inconsistent_positions: A litigant advances incompatible positions in the proceedings.
predicates.litigation_is_dishonestly_prolonged: The litigant’s conduct dishonestly causes the proceedings to continue for an extended period.

issues.definition: In appellate litigation, a court may impose costs when a litigant takes inconsistent positions and dishonestly prolongs the proceedings.
